newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Champagne shipwreck draws international interest.
newsitem.headline: Champagne shipwreck draws international interest.

text.p: Investors are flocking to help salvage a ship which was torpedoed in 1916 on its way to deliver champagne and cognac to the tsar's army and the Finnish central bank.

The consortium which discovered the wreck of the Jonkoping said on Friday it had been swamped with offers from U.S. and European financiers to help cover the cost of bringing up the 5,000 bottles of champagne and stores of cognac and wine which sank with the ship.

"We are fully covered for 50 percent of the total costs so far and we haven't invited more people into the project," said Claes Bergvall, one of the two Swedes who located the ship on the Baltic seafloor off Finland after reading about its fate in a book.
"We know we will be able to raise money," he told Reuters.

In the first two weeks of the salvage operation, divers have brought ashore some 500 bottles of champagne, a 1907 Heidsieck & Co which some say could fetch as much as 10,000 Swedish crowns ($1,240) per bottle.

London and Paris auction houses have contacted the consortium about selling the champagne, which has been kept in ideal conditions of complete darkness and one degree Celsius (34 Fahrenheit) and has kept its original light gold colour.
The divers, who can only spend 20 minutes at a time near the wreck 62 metres (200 feet) down on the ocean floor, will soon start raising the oak barrels of cognac.
They appear to be in good condition and, according to the ship's manifest, contain 40,000 litres of brandy.
The group are using a crane, ropes and an underwater camera to locate and raise the cargo distributed around the hold of the ship and over the seabed, and also including fine wines.
"Everything has been working according to plan except for the weather," Bergvall said.
The project will probably cost more than originally expected, but Bergvall has declined to give any figures.
The ketch lies some 25 nautical miles from Rauma, Finland, where it was headed when it was torpedoed during World War One. ($ = 8.019 Swedish Crowns)
